candidate_relations.reason: Fibro-osseous lesions are a distinct pathological category characterized by replacement of normal bone with fibrous tissue containing mineralized material. While they can produce calcified lesions in the maxilla, they are not odontogenic tumors and do not share the histological or clinical features of a complex odontoma (disorganized dental hard tissues). The clinical presentation with missing molar teeth and intraoral calcified mass strongly favors odontoma over a fibro-osseous lesion.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Fibro-osseous lesion is a broad category including ossifying fibroma, fibrous dysplasia, etc., not an odontoma

candidate_relations.reason: Calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumor (CEOT) is a benign but locally aggressive odontogenic neoplasm with characteristic amyloid-like material and Liesegang ring calcifications. While it can present with a calcified maxillary mass and associated unerupted/missing teeth in a young patient, it is a neoplasm of epithelial origin distinct from a complex odontoma, which is a hamartomatous malformation of all dental tissues. The dense amorphous irregular calcification and association with missing molars in a 13-year-old is more consistent with complex odontoma, making CEOT a conflicting subtype rather than equivalent.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: CEOT (Pindborg tumor) is a distinct odontogenic neoplasm, not an odontoma; both are odontogenic and calcified but represent incompatible subtypes

case_quality_flags: Classic complex odontoma presentation: adolescent, missing teeth, dense amorphous calcified mass in posterior maxilla
CEOT is a reasonable differential but represents an incompatible neoplastic subtype
